**What follows from the majority view.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the practical consequences. A Muslim's wealth can help him on that Day if he spent it in the way of Allah and on righteous causes, or left an ongoing charity (*ṣadaqah jāriyah*) — provided he dies upon Islam. If he was not a Muslim, or (Allah forbid) apostatised before death, none of his good deeds will benefit him. The same holds for children: a believer benefits from children who supplicate for his forgiveness after his death, and from the good they do if he tried to train them to be pious — that good keeps passing on to him. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that pious children may even obtain a parent's pardon by intercession, and mentions that a few reports speak of such intercession and its acceptance, particularly that of young children who had not yet reached puberty. (The commentary does not name the collections there, so we take it exactly as the commentary reports it and go no further.) The traffic runs the other way too: children who believed but whose deeds did not reach the level of their parents' may, on account of their parents' good deeds, be placed at their parents' high position — as in "We will join together with Our righteous servants their progeny" (52:21).

**And the hard limit.** All of that, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān stresses, is conditional on faith. Wherever the Qur'an or hadith says family connection will not avail on that Day, the reference is to non-believers — and the principle holds so absolutely that even the wife and children of a messenger do not benefit from his prophethood without faith: the son of Sayyidnā Nūḥ, the wife of Lūṭ, the father of Sayyidnā Ibrāhīm (peace be upon them). This is the theme behind "when the Trumpet is blown, there are no ties of kinship between them" (23:101), "the Day a man shall flee from his brother, and his mother and his father" (80:34–35), and "nor will a son be standing for his father in any way" (31:33).

**One small word.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notices that ayah 88 says *banūn* — a word literally restricted to *male* children. Probably, it suggests, because it is sons from whom effective help is expected in adverse situations; the expectation of that kind of rescue from daughters is rare even in this world. So the Qur'an names precisely the help you would have counted on — and cancels it. If even *they* cannot reach you there, nothing else in the ledger of worldly assets can.

## Ayah 91: the Fire is put on display

**"And the Hellfire will be displayed to the deviant."**

*Burrizat* — brought out into the open, made plainly visible. Ibn Kathir says "it will be shown to them," and then gives a detail that is hard to read calmly: "a neck will stretch forth from it, moaning and sighing, and their hearts will reach their throats."

We affirm this as it comes, without asking how and without emptying it of meaning. What the image conveys is that Hell is not an inert place waiting to be filled. It reaches. It makes a sound. And the physical response of the onlookers — hearts climbing into throats — is the Qur'an's picture of terror at its outer limit.

**The pairing is deliberate.** In ayah 90 the *muttaqīn* — those mindful of Allah — have Paradise carried towards them. In ayah 91 the *ghāwīn* — the astray, the deviant — have the Fire uncovered in front of them. Same Day, opposite ends. And in both cases the seeing comes *before* the entering: the believers behold their reward adorned and decorated; the astray behold their punishment before they are in it. Part of the reward is the sight; part of the punishment is the sight.

## Ayat 92–93: the question with no answer

**"And it will be said to them: 'Where are those you used to worship besides Allah? Can they help you or even help themselves?'"**

Ibn Kathir is precise about the tone: this is said to them "by way of reproach and rebuke." It is not a request for information. Everyone present knows the answer. The question exists to make them say it — or to make their silence say it.

The meaning, in Ibn Kathir's paraphrase: *the gods and idols you used to worship instead of Allah cannot help you today, and they cannot even protect themselves. You and they are fuel for Hell today, which you will surely enter.*

Sit with the structure of the challenge in ayah 93. It comes in two stages, and the second is the one that finishes the argument. First: *can they help you?* If a claimed deity fails that, it is useless. Then: *or can they even help themselves?* — which shows it was never a deity at all. A thing that cannot protect itself was never in a position to rescue anyone. The whole theology of the mushrikīn is dismantled in a single clause, on the spot, in front of the very objects of worship.

And notice where the question lands: it is asked *after* the Fire has been displayed (ayah 91). The interrogation comes when the consequence is already in view. There is no space left for argument, only for realisation.

## Ayat 94–95: hurled in, together

**"Then the idols will be hurled headlong into Hell, along with the deviant — and the soldiers of Iblīs, all together."**

The verb is *kubkibū*; Ibn Kathir renders the ayah, "Then they will be thrown on their faces into it (the Fire), they and the astray." Mujahid's gloss, reported by him, is blunt: "This means, they will be hurled into it." Others explained it as being thrown *on top of one another* — the disbelievers and their leaders who had called them to shirk, tumbling in together.

**Nobody is separated out.** The worshipped, the astray who worshipped them, and then, in ayah 95, "all of the hosts of Iblis together" — Ibn Kathir: "they will all be thrown into it." The object that was worshipped, the one who worshipped it, and the satanic host arrive in the same heap.

This is the exact reversal of what shirk promised. The whole point of the question in ayah 93 was help — *can they help you?* — and help is precisely what these worshipped things were adopted for. Ayah 94 shows the entire arrangement going over the edge at once. The one who was looked to for rescue does not stand apart from the one who looked; on one reading of the ayah, he lands on top of him.

## Living it

**Choose now what you want brought near then.** Ibn Kathir's definition of the people of Paradise is a test you can apply to an ordinary Tuesday: did you *prefer* it to whatever was in this world, and did you *strive* for it here? Neither half works alone.

**Audit the heart before the assets.** Ayat 88–89 do not say your wealth and children are worthless; on the majority reading they say those things are only worth what your faith makes them worth. The sound heart — free of shirk, testifying to Allah's Oneness, as Ibn ʿAbbās explained — is what converts a fortune into ṣadaqah jāriyah and a child into someone whose supplication still reaches you after death. Without it, the same fortune and the same child are counted with the *banūn* of ayah 88: precisely the help you expected, arriving as nothing.

**Ask ayah 93's question of yourself while answering still costs nothing.** *Can it help you, or can it even help itself?* Anything you lean on that would fail that test is being leaned on borrowed time. The question will be asked either way. The only variable is whether you get to answer it before the Fire is in view or after.

**Watch who is calling you.** On one explanation of ayah 94 reported by Ibn Kathir, those thrown on top of one another are the disbelievers together with the leaders who had called them to shirk. Following did not save the followers, and leading did not spare the leaders. Both ends of that chain arrive at the same place.

And the invitation in all of this is ayah 90. Paradise, adorned and decorated, is brought close to people who had already spent a lifetime choosing it over what was in front of them and working for it. That is a door that stands open now, while the choosing is still ours to make.

passages.title: The damned dispute with the gods they served
passages.tafsir:
These nine ayat let us listen in on a conversation in Hell. The people who worshipped something besides Allah, and the leaders and idols they worshipped, are thrown in together — and there they turn on one another. What holds the passage together is a single movement: a confession (97–98), a search for someone to blame (99), a search for someone to help (100–101), and finally a plea to be sent back (102) — every door tried, every door shut. Then ayah 103 calls all of it a sign, and ayah 104 closes on two of Allah's names.

## Ayah 96: they argue *inside* it

**قَالُوا وَهُمْ فِيهَا يَخْتَصِمُونَ** — "They will say, while they are contending in it…"

To hear this properly, hold on to where the ayat just before have left these people. Ibn Kathir describes the Fire being shown to them, a neck stretching forth from it, moaning and sighing, while their hearts reach their throats; they are asked, by way of reproach and rebuke, where the ones they used to worship instead of Allah are now — and told that those gods and idols cannot help them today and cannot even protect themselves. Then they are thrown in. That is the setting of ayah 96: not a courtroom with time to think, but the moment after the fall.

The verb here is from *khuṣūmah*, quarrel and litigation — not calm discussion, but the kind of arguing where each side is trying to fasten the blame onto the other. And notice the small phrase *wa hum fīhā*, "while they are in it." The dispute does not happen on the way to the Fire, as a last attempt to escape. It happens inside, when the argument can change nothing at all. Ibn Kathir connects this to Allah's words in Sūrah Ṣād: *Verily, that is the very truth — the mutual dispute of the people of the Fire* (38:64). Their quarrelling is itself part of the promised reality.

Ibn Kathir sketches how the argument opens: the weak ones among them say to their arrogant leaders, *"Verily, we were following you; can you avail us anything from the Fire?"* That is the instinct of every follower: the responsibility belongs upstream.

**Then something shifts.** Ibn Kathir's words are worth weighing: "Then they will realize that themselves are to blame and will say…" — and out comes the oath of ayah 97.

## Ayat 97–98: the confession, and what shirk actually was

**تَاللَّهِ إِن كُنَّا لَفِي ضَلَالٍ مُّبِينٍ** — "By Allah, we were truly in a manifest error."

They swear an oath — and they swear it *by Allah*. The One they refused to worship alone is now, in the Fire, the only One they think to swear by. And the error they confess is *mubīn*: manifest, open, obvious. Not a subtle mistake anyone could have made. The thing they could not see for a lifetime is unmissable now.

Ayah 98 tells us precisely what the error was: **إِذْ نُسَوِّيكُم بِرَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ** — "when we made you equal to the Lord of all worlds."

The verb **نُسَوِّي** is from *sawiya*, to level, to make even, to set two things on the same footing. This is the most important word in the passage, and it is worth being exact about what it means, because Ibn Kathir spells it out: *"we obeyed your commands as we should have obeyed the commands of the Lord of all that exists, and we worshipped you along with the Lord of all that exists."*

Two things stand out in that explanation.

**First, shirk here is a matter of obedience as much as ritual.** By Ibn Kathir's wording, the first half of their crime was giving another's command the weight that only the command of the Lord of all that exists may have. Whatever we obey unconditionally — a leader, a crowd, a custom, an appetite — is being set on a level it does not belong on.

**Second, the wording is "along with."** Ibn Kathir's gloss is not that they replaced Allah, but that they worshipped these others *alongside* Him. Adding a partner is not a small adjustment; the passage calls it manifest error, because *Rabb al-ʿĀlamīn*, the Lord of every world, is the One with whom nothing can be levelled.

## Ayah 99: "no one led us astray but the criminals"

**وَمَا أَضَلَّنَا إِلَّا الْمُجْرِمُونَ.** Ibn Kathir's gloss is spare: "nobody called us to do that except the evildoers."

It is a true statement and a useless one. On the earlier ayah about being thrown into the Fire, Ibn Kathir relays a further comment from unnamed others — "They will be thrown on top of one another, the disbelievers and their leaders who called them to Shirk" — so those leaders really did call them to it, and are heaped in with them. But naming who invited you does not undo what you accepted. Note the order the passage keeps: the followers first admit *we* were in manifest error (97), and only then point at the criminals (99). Even here, the accusation comes after the confession — and it saves nobody.

## Ayat 100–101: no intercessor, no friend

**فَمَا لَنَا مِن شَافِعِينَ ۝ وَلَا صَدِيقٍ حَمِيمٍ** — "Now we have no intercessors, nor a close friend."

Ibn Kathir pairs this with what the people of the Fire say in Sūrah al-Aʿrāf: *…now are there any intercessors for us that they might intercede on our behalf? Or could we be sent back so that we might do deeds other than those deeds which we used to do?* (7:53). The same two hopes, in the same order, in both places — and the second of them is exactly what ayah 102 is about to voice.

Notice how the wording narrows. *Shāfiʿīn* is plural — no intercessors at all, not one among the many they had counted on. Then even the singular is gone: not one *ṣadīq ḥamīm*, not a single close friend. The idols cannot intercede; the leaders they followed are in the same Fire; the crowd that once made their religion feel obvious has dissolved into a quarrel.

This does not mean that help in the Hereafter is unreal — only that it runs through faith. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that a Muslim's wealth can benefit him there if he spent it in the way of Allah or in ongoing charity (*ṣadaqah jāriyah*), and that his children can benefit him if they supplicate for him after his death or continue doing the good he raised them to do; it also mentions that a few narrations report the acceptance of such intercession, especially the intercession of young children who had not yet reached puberty. (The bundle before us does not name a collection for those narrations, so neither will we.) It cites *We will join together with Our righteous servants their progeny* (52:21) for the reverse direction: believing children whose deeds fell short of their parents' may be raised to their parents' rank.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then draws the principle out plainly: wherever the Qur'an or hadith says family connection will be of no avail in the Hereafter, the reference is to the disbelievers. It holds even at the highest level — even the wife or child of a messenger, if they are not believers, does not benefit from his prophethood; the examples given are the son of Sayyidnā Nūḥ (peace be upon him), the wife of Lūṭ (peace be upon him) and the father of Sayyidnā Ibrāhīm (peace be upon him). In each case the relative was not a believer, and nearness to a prophet did not save them. It is the same truth as *there are no ties of kinship between them* (23:101), *upon the day when a man shall flee from his brother, his mother, his father* (80:34–35), and *nor will a son be standing for his father in any way* (31:33).

That is what makes ayah 101 so bleak. Not merely "no friend helped us" — no friend *is there* to help.

## Ayah 102: the wish to go back

**فَلَوْ أَنَّ لَنَا كَرَّةً فَنَكُونَ مِنَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ** — "(Alas!) If we only had a chance to return, we shall truly be among the believers!"

*Karrah* is a turn back, a second run at it. Every door has now closed except this one, and they push on it too.

Ibn Kathir's comment is the sharpest sentence in the passage, and it should be read slowly: they will wish that they could come back to this world so that they could do deeds of obedience to their Lord — **as they claim** — but Allah knows that if they were to come back to this world, they would only go back to doing forbidden things, and He knows that they are liars.

So this is not a repentance that came slightly too late. By Ibn Kathir's reading it is not repentance at all: the claim is refused because the One who hears it knows what they would actually do with a second life. The window for faith is the window we are standing in right now.

## Ayah 103: the sign

**إِنَّ فِي ذَٰلِكَ لَآيَةً ۖ وَمَا كَانَ أَكْثَرُهُم مُّؤْمِنِينَ** — "Verily, in this is indeed a sign, yet most of them are not believers."

Ibn Kathir explains that the sign lies in the dispute of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) with his people and his proof of Tawhid — clear evidence that there is no god but Allah. So the sign is not only the scene in the Fire; it is the whole argument Ibrahim (peace be upon him) put to his people, still standing. And still, "most of them are not believers." Evidence is not the missing ingredient. It never was.

## Ayah 104: the closing words

**وَإِنَّ رَبَّكَ لَهُوَ الْعَزِيزُ الرَّحِيمُ** — "And verily, your Lord, He is truly the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful."

The passage that opened with the Fire in full view ends by naming the Lord with these two names together. The tafsir material in front of us gives the ayah and its translation and adds no comment on the two names, so we will not put words in its mouth. What we can simply notice is the placement: after a scene in which every other refuge fails, the last word of the passage is about Him, and it holds might and mercy in the same breath.

## Living it

The passage hands us three things to actually do.

**Audit what you obey, not just what you call worship.** Ibn Kathir defined the levelling of ayah 98 as obeying another's command the way the command of the Lord of all that exists should be obeyed. Nobody in this scene thought of themselves as an idolater; they thought of themselves as loyal followers. The question to ask is where a human voice — a leader, a family expectation, a peer group, a market — is currently being given the final word.

**Stop banking on people.** Ayat 100–101 strip away intercessors and friends alike. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's point is that such help works only through faith: charity sent ahead, children who pray for you, good you trained them to keep doing. Relationships are not useless in the Hereafter — but they carry nothing on their own.

**Treat this life as the second chance you would have asked for.** Ayah 102 is a request for exactly the circumstances you are in right now: time, a working body, and the ability to choose faith. Ibn Kathir says that request is refused there — and it is already granted here.

The closing note of ayah 103 — "yet most of them are not believers" — is not only about them. It is a warning that clarity does not automatically produce faith. Something has to be done with what has been seen.

passages.title: Noah, the trustworthy messenger who asks no reward
passages.tafsir:
**The passage in brief.** These six ayat open the story of Nuh (Noah), peace be upon him: his people rejected him, and in reply he set before them a short, complete case for listening to a messenger — a call to fear Allah, a statement that he is trustworthy with the message he carries, and a declaration that he wants no payment from them. The passage is held together by one repeated command: *"So fear Allah, and obey me"* — said once in ayah 108 and again in ayah 110, with one reason placed on either side of it.

## Who Nuh was, and what he walked into

Ibn Kathir opens his comment on this passage by placing Nuh at the very beginning of prophetic history: Allah tells us here about His servant and Messenger Nuh, peace be upon him, **the first Messenger sent by Allah to the people of the earth after they had started to worship idols**. Allah sent him to forbid that, and to warn people of the consequences of idol worship.

That single sentence changes how you hear the passage. Nuh is not correcting a stray habit in an otherwise sound society; idol worship had already taken hold among people, and he is the first messenger sent against it. Everything he says in these ayat is said into that situation.

And, Ibn Kathir notes, his people belied him and continued their practice of worshipping idols besides Allah.

## "They rejected the messengers" — why the plural? (ayah 105)

Ayah 105 says the people of Nuh rejected **al-mursalīn**, "the messengers" — plural. Ibn Kathir explains the wording directly: Allah revealed that **their disbelieving in him was akin to disbelieving in all the Messengers**.

This is a principle worth holding on to. To reject the messenger standing in front of you is, in Allah's own reckoning, to have rejected the messengers as such — because what you have refused is the very thing that makes a messenger a messenger. So the Qur'an does not say "they rejected Nuh." It says they rejected *the messengers*.

## "Their brother Nuh" (ayah 106)

Ayah 106 introduces him with a striking word: *"when their brother Nuh said to them."* Not "a man came to them," not "a stranger warned them." He is **their brother** — one of their own people, addressed to them from among them.

Ibn Kathir returns to something close to this at the end of the passage, when he paraphrases the force of Nuh's closing appeal as: *it is clear to you that I am telling the truth and that I am faithfully fulfilling the mission with which Allah has entrusted me.* What he was asking them to accept was not obscure to them.

## "Will you not fear Allah?" — the word *taqwa*

His first word to them is a question, not an accusation: **a-lā tattaqūn**, "will you not have *taqwa*?"

*Taqwa* is one of the great Qur'anic words. It is usually translated "fear of Allah," though the fear it names is not panic but the alert, protective awareness of a person who guards himself before his Lord. Ibn Kathir gives the question its precise content in this setting: it means **"do you not fear Allah when you worship others instead of Him?"**

So the *taqwa* Nuh calls for here is not a vague religious feeling. It is the awareness of Allah that stands directly opposed to worshipping anything besides Him. Nuh does not begin by listing rules; he begins by trying to wake that awareness in them.

Notice also the form of it: a question, addressed to them, inviting them to answer for themselves. The first move of the preaching recorded in this passage is appeal, not condemnation.

## "I am a trustworthy messenger to you" (ayah 107) — the meaning of *amīn*

Nuh describes himself with one adjective: **amīn**, trustworthy — one who can be entrusted with something.

Ibn Kathir gives it a very exact sense. It means: *"I am the Messenger of Allah to you, faithfully fulfilling the mission with which Allah has sent me. I convey the Messages of my Lord to you, and I do not add anything to them or take anything away from them."*

That definition is worth sitting with, because it is narrower and stronger than the general English "honest." Being *amīn* as a messenger is about the **message as a trust** placed in his hands. A trust is something you hold for someone else and hand over exactly as you received it. Nuh is telling them: nothing has been added to this, and nothing has been taken away from it. What reaches your ears is what came from his Lord.

## "I ask you no reward for it" (ayah 109)

Then the second credential, and it is a negative one — what he does *not* want from them. Ibn Kathir renders the sense plainly: *"I do not want any payment for the advice I give you; I will save my reward for it with Allah."*

The ayah's own wording carries this: his reward is only from **the Lord of all that exists**. He has not given up payment; he has left it with Allah. The One who sent him is the One who will reward him.

This dismantles the standard suspicion levelled at anyone who calls people to change: *what is he getting out of this?* Nuh removes the answer in advance. There is no fee.

**The ruling the scholars drew from this.** Maarif ul Quran takes a legal point from ayah 109: it is learnt from this verse that charging and accepting wages for religious teaching and preaching is not right. On this the generations differed — **the righteous elders ruled it forbidden, while the later generations allowed it under compelling circumstances.** Maarif ul Quran adds that the full details are given under its explanation of *"do not take a paltry price for My signs"* (2:41), and does not take the discussion further here.

Since the two positions are reported side by side, they are best left as reported rather than resolved. What the passage itself holds up is unmistakable: a caller whose message is manifestly not for sale.

## Why "So fear Allah, and obey me" is said twice (ayat 108 and 110)

The most obvious feature of the passage is its repetition. The same sentence — **fa-ttaqū'llāha wa aṭīʿūn**, "So fear Allah, and obey me" — appears in ayah 108 and again in ayah 110, once after "I am a trustworthy messenger to you" and once after "I ask you no reward."

Maarif ul Quran explains this in its "Special note": the sentence is repeated twice to make clear that **either one of the two qualities on its own would have been enough** to require fear of Allah and obedience to the messenger — first, his honesty and integrity (ayah 107); second, his teaching and preaching without a fee (ayah 109). And when the Messenger combines all these traits in himself, obedience to him and fear of his Lord become all the more necessary.

So the repetition is not emphasis for its own sake; it is the shape of the argument. Read it as two complete cases:

- *I am trustworthy with what I have been given* → **so fear Allah, and obey me.**
- *I want nothing from you for it* → **so fear Allah, and obey me.**

**And notice what the two commands are.** "Fear Allah" and "obey me" arrive joined, in that order. The obedience Nuh asks for rests on the *taqwa* named first — the same awareness of Allah he tried to wake in them in ayah 106. And yet obedience to the messenger is genuinely part of what is asked, not an optional extra: rejecting him, as Ibn Kathir says, amounted to rejecting all the Messengers.

## Living it

**Judge a message by what its carrier wants from you.** These ayat give the believer a plain test, and it is a test Nuh volunteered himself for. Is the person calling you handling the message as a trust — passing it on without adding anything to it and without taking anything away from it? And is he asking for something in return? Nuh's two credentials in ayat 107 and 109 remain two good questions to ask of anyone who speaks to you in the name of religion.

**And take the same test yourself.** Whoever conveys anything of the religion — a parent teaching a child, a friend passing on what they learned — stands under the standard set in ayah 107: convey it as it came, adding nothing and dropping nothing, especially not the parts that are hard to say. Where you have no knowledge, the honest form of trustworthiness is to say so.

**Preach without a price tag.** Whatever the scholars concluded about permissibility under compelling circumstances, the disposition the passage praises is clear: the caller who leaves his reward with Allah rather than seeking it from the people he is calling.

**Start where Nuh started.** He did not open with argument or rebuke. He opened with *"will you not fear Allah?"* — a question aimed at reviving someone's awareness of their Lord. And the Qur'an frames him, even before those who would reject him, as their brother.

passages.title: "Shall we believe when the lowest follow you?"
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

This is the moment the argument against Nuh (peace be upon him) stops being about the message and becomes about the people who accepted it. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, the disbelievers rejected his invitation to faith "on the plea that his followers were worthless poor people." Ayat 111–115 hold together as one exchange — a single objection in ayah 111, and a fourfold answer in ayat 112–115 that refuses their premise, hands the reckoning back to Allah, refuses their offer, and closes by naming exactly what a prophet is and is not.

## The objection: snobbery dressed as reasoning

Ayah 111 gives their words: **قَالُوٓاْ أَنُؤۡمِنُ لَكَ وَٱتَّبَعَكَ ٱلۡأَرۡذَلُونَ** — "Shall we believe in you, when the inferior follow you?" Ibn Kathir unpacks what lies underneath the question: "We do not believe in you, and we will not follow you and become equal to the meanest of the people, who follow you and believe in you, and they are the lowest among us."

Notice what their objection is *not*. It is not "your message is false." It is not "your signs are unconvincing." It is a statement about seating arrangements. The sticking point is *becoming equal* — joining a body of people they had already ranked beneath themselves. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān catches the tone exactly: how could they, "the elite and noble, mix up with them?"

The word they choose is **ٱلۡأَرۡذَلُونَ**, rendered in our sources as "the inferior," "the lowest," "the meanest," "the lowest people." Our sources treat it as exactly that — a *label* they put on his followers, in the phrase of Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, "the label of sordidness." And as we will see, it is a label they had no basis to attach.

## The first answer: "That is not my file to open"

Ayah 112: **قَالَ وَمَآ عِلۡمِي بِمَا كَانُواْ يَعۡمَلُونَ** — "And what knowledge have I of what they used to do?"

Ibn Kathir explains the sense: "what does it have to do with me if they follow me? No matter what they used to do before, I do not have to check on them and examine their background; all I have to do is accept it if they believe in me; whatever is in their hearts is for Allah to know."

This is worth sitting with, because it is easy to misread the reply as a concession — as if Nuh (peace be upon him) were saying, "you may be right about them, but I did not check." That is not it. On Ibn Kathir's reading he is refusing the whole framework. Vetting people's pasts and reading their hearts is simply not part of his commission. His door is open on one condition: belief. What a person was before, what they carry inside, what they may still be working through — that is a matter between them and Allah, and Nuh (peace be upon him) does not appoint himself its inspector.

There is a second, quieter edge to the reply, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws it out. In saying "I do not know about what they do," Nuh (peace be upon him) is "thereby hinting that their understanding of nobility on the basis of family background, wealth, or status was wrong, and that the nobility or meanness and honour or disgrace is dependent on one's deeds and morals." In other words: you have called them the lowest — on what evidence? You have measured them by lineage and wealth, which are not the measure at all. The real measure is deeds and character, and of *that* I claim no inventory.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds, citing Qurtubi: "Hence, it was their ignorance to put the label of sordidness on his followers, because they did not know about their deeds and disposition. Unless one knows fully well about the morals and deeds of others, it is not right to pass any judgment about them."

Two principles come out of that, and they are worth separating:

- **Rank is earned by deeds and morals, not inherited from family, wealth, or status.** That is the heading Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives this passage. The elite had a ranking system, and it was simply the wrong instrument for the thing they were trying to measure.
- **Judgement requires knowledge you almost never have.** Their contempt was not merely unkind; it was *uninformed* — they did not know about the deeds and disposition of the people they were dismissing. Qurtubi's rule is strict: without full knowledge of someone's morals and deeds, passing judgement on them is not right.

## Ayah 113: the reckoning belongs to Allah

**إِنۡ حِسَابُهُمۡ إِلَّا عَلَىٰ رَبِّيۖ لَوۡ تَشۡعُرُونَ** — "Their account is only with my Lord, if you could (but) know," or, in our other rendering, "Their judgment is with my Lord, if you had any sense!"

Having said that examining people's records is not his commission, Nuh (peace be upon him) says where those records are actually kept. Ibn Kathir's comment on the previous ayah had already pointed in this direction — "whatever is in their hearts is for Allah to know" — and this ayah states it outright: their account rests with his Lord, and with no one else. The sentence then turns back to the objectors themselves, closing on their own lack of understanding rather than on the standing of the believers they had dismissed.

## Ayah 114: the offer he would not take

**وَمَآ أَنَا۠ بِطَارِدِ ٱلۡمُؤۡمِنِينَ** — "And I am not going to drive away the believers."

Ibn Kathir reads a proposal behind this refusal: "It seems that they asked him to drive these people away, then they would follow him, but he refused to do that."

That is the sharpest thing in the passage. On this reading they were not just sneering; they were *bargaining*. Clear the poor believers out of the room, and we will join. From a purely numerical view it is a tempting trade — swap a handful of the powerless for the leadership of a whole society. He refused.

And look at how the two groups are named. They had called them **ٱلۡأَرۡذَلُونَ**, "the lowest." Nuh (peace be upon him) calls them **ٱلۡمُؤۡمِنِينَ**, "the believers." That is the only label he recognises, and it is the one that settles their worth. The moment a person believes, they are not a bargaining chip. A community built by evicting the sincere in order to attract the influential would not be Allah's community at all.

## Ayah 115: the job description that ends the argument

**إِنۡ أَنَا۠ إِلَّا نَذِيرٞ مُّبِينٞ** — "I am only a plain warner," or "I am only sent with a clear warning."

This is the sentence that makes all the others make sense. Ibn Kathir gives the meaning: "I have been sent as a warner, and whoever obeys me and follows me and believes in me, then he belongs to me and I to him, whether he is noble or common, upper-class or lower-class."

Nuh's whole authority and his whole limitation sit in that one description. He is not a gatekeeper who screens applicants. He is not a judge who assigns final worth. He is not a recruiter building a coalition of the useful. He delivers a clear warning; whoever responds is his, and he is theirs.

That last phrase in Ibn Kathir's gloss is remarkably warm: *he belongs to me and I to him*. The relationship runs both ways, and it runs identically for the noble and the common, the upper-class and the lower-class. Social rank does not survive contact with that sentence. It is not softened or balanced — it is simply not a category in the exchange.

## The shape of the reply

Read the four ayat together and you can see the objection being dismantled joint by joint:

1. **112 — I do not run background checks.** Examining people's backgrounds is not my commission.
2. **113 — Allah does the reckoning.** Their account is only with my Lord.
3. **114 — I will not expel a believer to gain you.** Faith makes a person non-negotiable.
4. **115 — I am only a plain warner.** This is what I am; everything above follows from it.

He never insults them back, and he never defends his followers by listing their virtues — which would have accepted their game. He removes the game from the table.

## Living it

**Do not rank the believers.** The elite among the people of Nuh (peace be upon him) had a mental league table, and that table is exactly what kept them out of faith. Whenever we find ourselves reluctant to sit, pray, marry, or work alongside another believer because of their background, income, accent, caste, family name or profession, we are holding the same table they held. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's heading for this passage says it plainly: nobility of a person depends on deeds and moral qualities, not on family or status.

**Do not audit anyone's past at the door.** The answer of Nuh (peace be upon him) — "what knowledge have I of what they used to do?" — is a model for how to receive someone who has just turned toward Allah. Their history is not our file. Ibn Kathir puts our whole duty in one clause: *all I have to do is accept it if they believe*. Whatever is in the heart is for Allah to know.

**Restrain the verdict.** Qurtubi's rule, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān transmits it, is a discipline for the tongue and the mind alike: unless you know fully well about someone's morals and deeds, it is not right to pass judgement on them. Most of our low opinions of other people are formed on far less information than that.

**Refuse the trade.** Every community faces some version of the offer that Nuh (peace be upon him) refused — quietly sidelining the poor, the awkward, the newly practising, in the hope of attracting the influential. His answer, made when the leadership of the whole society was on the other side of it, was simply: *I am not going to drive away the believers.*

**Know what you are.** Ayah 115 is a liberating limit for anyone who calls others to Allah — a parent, a teacher, a friend. Your task is to convey the warning clearly and to keep the door open. You are not the judge of who deserves to be inside, and you are not the one who holds the reckoning. That, as ayah 113 says, is only with your Lord.

passages.title: Noah's prayer and the drowning of his people
passages.tafsir:
This passage is the end of the story of Nuh (peace be upon him) as Surah al-Shuʿarāʾ tells it: his people finally threaten to stone him, he turns from them to his Lord in prayer, and Allah answers — the ark carries the believers to safety and the water closes over everyone else. Ibn Kathir gathers the whole passage under one heading: *His People's Threat, Nuh's Prayer Against Them, and Their Destruction*. That is the movement of these seven ayat. Ayah 116 is the threat, 117–118 the prayer, 119–120 the answer, and 121–122 the lesson Allah draws from it.

## The years behind ayah 116

Ibn Kathir sets the scene before he explains a single word. Nuh, he says, stayed among his people for a long time, calling them to Allah night and day, in secret and openly. That is the background hum behind ayah 116: not a brief mission, but a long stretch of patient invitation, tried in every manner a caller could try — private conversation and public appeal, daylight and darkness.

And the result? Ibn Kathir puts it with painful clarity: the more he repeated his call to them, the more determined they were to cling to their extreme disbelief and resist his call. His persistence did not soften them. By Ibn Kathir's account, it is precisely as that resistance hardened that they arrived, "in the end," at the threat.

**"If you do not desist, O Nuh"** — Ibn Kathir glosses the phrase exactly: *if you do not stop calling us to your religion*. Notice what they are asking for. Not a different argument, not evidence — simply silence. They do not answer the message; they demand its end.

**"you will surely be among *al-marjūmīn*"** — those who are stoned. Ibn Kathir's gloss is blunt: *we will stone you*. The phrasing is chilling in its casualness — you will be counted among the stoned, as though there were an established category of people dealt with that way and Nuh would simply be added to the list. After all that night-and-day calling, this is the argument they arrive at: rocks.

## "Shall we believe in you while the lowest people follow you?"

A few ayat earlier (111–112) they had given their real objection, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses on it because it explains the contempt behind the threat. They rejected Nuh's invitation on the plea that his followers were worthless poor people — how could they, the elite and the noble, mix with such company?

Nuh's answer in ayah 112 is a masterpiece of restraint: *"I do not know about what they do."* He does not defend his followers' social standing, because that was never the measure. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the hint: their whole idea of nobility — reckoned by family background, wealth, or status — was wrong. Nobility or meanness, honour or disgrace, depends on a person's deeds and morals. So it was sheer ignorance for them to stamp the label of lowliness on his followers, since they knew nothing of those people's deeds and disposition. And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Qurtubi, turns this into a rule that outlives the story: unless you know someone's morals and deeds fully, it is not right to pass judgment on them.

Keep that in view as you read ayah 118, where Nuh asks Allah to save "those of the believers who are with me." The very people dismissed as the dregs of society are the ones the ark is built for.

## The prayer: ayat 117–118

Ibn Kathir marks the turning point precisely: *at that point* — when the threat of stoning was made — *he prayed against them, and Allah responded to his prayer*. The prayer comes after the door has been shut from the other side, not before.

**"My Lord! My people have truly rejected me."** In ayah 117 Nuh does not open with a list of injuries — the mockery, the long years, the threat of stoning. He states one thing: *"My Lord! Verily, my people have denied me."* And he calls them *qawmī*, "my people" — his own folk, his own kin. The wound he names is not to his body but to the message he carried and to the bond he shared with them.

**"So judge between me and them decisively."** Ibn Kathir renders ayah 118 "judge You between me and them" — a request that Allah Himself now settle the case that human argument could not settle. Nuh does not name a punishment or dictate a method; he hands the matter over and asks only that it be decided, and decided conclusively.

Ibn Kathir sets this beside another prayer of Nuh in the Qur'an: *"Then he invoked his Lord (saying): 'I have been overcome, so help (me)!'"* (54:10). Read together, the two show the same man in the same place — a servant who has genuinely reached the end of what he can do, saying so plainly to his Lord, and asking Him to take over.

**"and save me and the believers with me."** Even in the prayer that calls down judgment, Nuh's request is fundamentally about rescue — his own and that of the small band who believed. The two halves of ayah 118 belong together: a decisive verdict, and safety for the faithful within it.

## The answer: ayat 119–120

Ayah 119 answers the prayer almost word for word. He asked, "save me and the believers with me"; Allah says, *"So We saved him and those with him."* The request comes back as an accomplished fact.

**"the fully loaded Ark"** — Ibn Kathir explains that a "laden ship" is one filled with cargo, and with the couples, one pair from every species, that were carried in it. So the word is not decorative. It tells you the ark was packed and provisioned: the believers, their goods, and the breeding pairs from which life on earth would begin again.

Ayah 120 then closes the account: *"Then afterwards We drowned the rest."* Ibn Kathir's summary is total on both sides — *We saved Nuh and all of those who followed him, and We drowned those who disbelieved in him and went against his commands, all of them.* Not most. All. And note the sequence the ayah itself insists on: *then, afterwards.* The rescue came first; the drowning came after. The believers were secured before the judgment fell.

## The lesson: ayat 121–122

**"Surely in this is a sign."** In ayah 121 Allah calls the whole episode a sign. History here is not merely something that happened; it is something set down to be read. A prophet threatened, a prayer answered, a rescue and a ruin: whoever reads that pattern honestly learns something about how Allah deals with truth and with those who fight it.

**"Yet most of them would not believe."** And still — the sign is there, plain and enormous, and most do not believe. Set against ayah 116, the line is quietly devastating: Nuh called night and day, in secret and openly, for a long time, and the response was hardening, not faith. Small numbers, then, have never been evidence that a message is false.

**"And your Lord is certainly the Almighty, Most Merciful."** Ayah 122 closes with two of Allah's names side by side, and the pairing is the point.

*Al-ʿAzīz*, the All-Mighty: the One whose might nothing resists. The people who threatened to stone Nuh were answered by water they could not argue with. The family background, wealth, and status by which they measured themselves weighed nothing against it.

*Al-Raḥīm*, the Most Merciful: and the very same event that displays His might displays His mercy. The flood that drowned the deniers is the flood the ark rode. Nuh and the believers were carried through it, provisioned, in a laden ship, into a new world. One act of Allah, two names — and both describe Him truly.

Notice, too, that Allah says *"your Lord"* — addressing the Prophet ﷺ directly. The Lord who was mighty on Nuh's behalf and merciful to the believers with him is *your* Lord, the same One, unchanged. That is much of the point of telling the story.

## Living it

**Say what is true and leave the outcome to Allah.** Nuh called night and day, in secret and openly, for a long time, and hearts only hardened. He was not a failed caller; he was a faithful one. Our task is the calling.

**Bring the complaint to the right place.** When Nuh reached the end, he did not answer threat with threat. He turned and said, *"My Lord, my people have denied me."* The complaint went upward. That direction, in the hardest moment of a long life, is what the passage models.

**Stop measuring people by status.** The elite of Nuh's people were sure that poor followers discredited the message; Allah put those followers in the ark and drowned the rest. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, quoting Qurtubi, gives the practical form of it: unless you know a person's morals and deeds fully, it is not right to pass judgment on them. Most of the contempt we carry for others fails that test on the first line.

**Hold both names together.** Ayah 122 names Allah *al-ʿAzīz* and *al-Raḥīm* in one breath — and the story just told shows both in one moment.

passages.title: Hūd's address to the people of ʿĀd
passages.tafsir:
This passage is the sermon of the Prophet Hūd (peace be upon him) to his people ʿĀd — a nation described in the sources as physically strong, very tall and very violent, and given a great deal of provision. What holds the passage together is a single, tightly built speech: Hūd opens by establishing who he is and what he wants (123–127), then names three specific sins (128–130), then repeats his call and turns their own blessings into the argument against them (131–134), before closing with a warning (135).

## Who ʿĀd were

Ibn Kathir tells us that Hūd's people lived in **al-Aḥqāf** — the curved sand-hills near Ḥaḍramawt, on the borders of Yemen — and that they lived after the time of Nūḥ (peace be upon him). He cites Sūrat al-Aʿrāf, where Allah reminds them: *"And remember that He made you successors after the people of Nūḥ and increased you amply in stature"* (7:69). That increase, Ibn Kathir explains, refers to the fact that they were physically strong and well-built, very tall, and very violent. Alongside that, they had been given a great deal of provision — wealth, gardens, rivers, sons, crops and fruits.

That is the crucial background. Everything Hūd is about to criticise, and everything he is about to list as a blessing, comes out of that one fact: they were given a great deal. "Yet despite all of that," writes Ibn Kathir, "they worshipped others besides Allah." So Allah sent Hūd — **one of their own** — as a Messenger bringing them good news and delivering warnings, calling them to worship Allah alone and warning them of Allah's wrath and punishment if they were to go against him and treat him harshly.

## "Their brother Hūd" (124)

Ayah 124 does not say "a messenger came to them"; it says *their brother Hūd*. Ibn Kathir stresses the same point in his own words: Allah sent Hūd, **one of their own**. And his first words are not an accusation but a question: **"Will you not fear Allah?"** — which Ibn Kathir renders, keeping the Arabic term, *"Will you not have Taqwa?"* It is an invitation before it is a rebuke.

Then come three short statements that form the standard credentials of a messenger:

- **"I am truly a trustworthy messenger to you"** (125) — in Ibn Kathir's rendering, *"Verily, I am a trustworthy Messenger to you."*
- **"So fear Allah, and obey me"** (126). Ibn Kathir glosses this simply: *"Worship your Lord and obey your Messenger."* Notice the pairing — the call to fear Allah and the call to obey the one Allah sent arrive together, in a single breath.
- **"I do not ask you for any reward for this"** (127). His reward, as Ibn Kathir puts it, "is only from the Lord of all that exists." He asks nothing at all from the people he is calling.

Ibn Kathir notes that Hūd said to them what Nūḥ (peace be upon him) had said to his people — the same call, delivered to a different generation.

## The three charges (128–130)

**"˹Why˺ do you build a landmark on every high place in vanity?"** (128)

Ibn Kathir reports that the scholars of tafsir differed over the word **rīʿ**. Summarising them, he says it refers to an elevated location at a well-known crossroads, where ʿĀd would build a huge, dazzling, sturdy structure. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the difference more precisely: Ibn Jarīr relates from Mujāhid that a *rīʿ* is the passage between two hills, while Ibn ʿAbbās and the majority took it to mean a **high place** — the same root gives *rīʿ al-nabāt*, growing and climbing vegetation, i.e. what rises.

The word **āyah** literally means a symbol or a sign; here, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, it means a high palace. Ibn Kathir renders it "a well-known landmark." So the picture is of a people who put a monument on every prominent rise — not one great building, but *every* height claimed and marked.

And **taʿbathūn**: Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces it to *ʿabath*, which means something of no value or benefit — not in reality and not even by implication. On that reading, the verse means they used to make very high palaces of no benefit, which they did not need; it was just to fulfil their ego and pride. Ibn Kathir's paraphrase is blunt in the same direction: *"you are only doing that for the purpose of frivolity, not because you need it, but for fun and to show off your strength."* He then explains why a prophet would trouble himself to denounce architecture: it was a waste of time, it exhausted people's bodies for no purpose, and it kept them busy with something of no benefit in this world or the next.

**"And construct castles, as if you are going to live forever"** (129)

**Masāniʿ** is the plural of *masnaʿ*. Qatādah understood it as a water tank; Mujāhid took it to mean a strong palace — and Ibn Kathir quotes Mujāhid's fuller wording: *"fortresses built up strong and high and structures that are built to last."* Both readings are transmitted; Mujāhid's puts the weight on durability, on something built to outlast its builder.

The final clause is where the whole verse turns. Imam al-Bukhari comments in *Sahih al-Bukhari* that the word *laʿalla* is used here as a word of simile, and that Ibn ʿAbbās rendered it *ka-annakum takhludūn* — **"as if you were going to live forever."** (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports this citing *Rūḥ al-Maʿānī*.) On that reading the verse is not reporting a belief in immortality; it is describing how they *behaved*. Ibn Kathir draws out the aim behind the building: it was "so that you may stay there forever, but that is not going to happen, because they will eventually cease to be, just as happened in the case of those who came before you."

**"And act so viciously when you attack ˹others˺"** (130)

The ayah says that when they seized someone, they seized **as jabbārīn** — tyrants. Ibn Kathir's comment is short and total: they are described as being strong, violent and tyrannical.

Notice how all three charges run back to the same surplus that Ibn Kathir set out at the beginning: great physical strength and a great deal of provision. Strength with nothing needing to be built produces monuments for show; abundance produces fortresses meant to last forever; power with no restraint produces the seizing of ayah 130. Hūd is not listing three unrelated habits so much as showing one people spending one gift in three wrong directions.

## What the Sunnah says about building beyond need

Ayah 129 carries a practical ruling, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws it out: the construction of houses and buildings **without need** is a condemnable act. It supports this with a hadith quoted by Imam Tirmidhi on the authority of Anas (may Allah be pleased with him): *"All spendings are in Allah's way, except construction, which has no merit"* — meaning, as the commentary explains, that a building constructed in excess of requirement has no benefit or virtue. Another narration from Anas (may Allah be pleased with him), which the commentary cites without naming a collection, confirms the same: *"Every building is a tribulation for the builder, except that which is necessary, because it is not a nuisance."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān further cites *Rūḥ al-Maʿānī* to the effect that without genuine requirement the construction of tall buildings is contemptible and condemned under the Sharīʿah of the Prophet ﷺ.

Read this carefully and fairly. The condemnation attaches to **excess beyond need** — what is necessary is explicitly excluded in the second narration, and the commentary's whole framing is "in excess of requirement."

## The blessings become the argument (131–134)

In ayah 131 Hūd repeats, word for word, the appeal he already made in 126: **"So fear Allah, and obey me."** The repetition is deliberate — the charges in 128–130 sit *inside* the two calls, framed on both sides by the same invitation. He is not building a case for the prosecution; he is trying to bring them home.

Then, as Ibn Kathir puts it, "Hūd began reminding them of the blessings that Allah had bestowed upon them." Ayah 132 is remarkable in how it names Allah: not by a title, but by an act — **"Fear the One Who has provided you with ˹the good˺ things you know."** Ibn Kathir renders the verb as "aided you with." And *bimā taʿlamūn* — "with what you yourselves know" — appeals to nothing they could dispute. He is not asking them to accept a report; he is pointing at their own inventory.

Then he itemises it (133–134): **cattle and children, gardens and springs.** These are the very things Ibn Kathir listed at the outset as the provision ʿĀd had been given — wealth, gardens, rivers, sons, crops and fruits — and gardens and springs mean food and water in a land of sand-hills. Every one of these was theirs to be proud of, and Hūd's argument is that each of them arrived from Someone. The same list that fed their pride is the evidence for their obligation.

## "I truly fear for you the torment of a tremendous day" (135)

Hūd's closing line is not framed as a threat but as a **fear** — *innī akhāfu ʿalaykum*, "I fear **for** you." That is a brother's language, matching the "their brother Hūd" of ayah 124. Ibn Kathir explains the condition attached: this is what awaits "if you disbelieve and oppose (your Prophet)."

And then Ibn Kathir's summary of the whole speech, which is also its sorrow: "So he called them to Allah with words of encouragement and words of warning, **but it was to no avail.**" Everything a caller could offer — kinship, integrity, no fee, reasoned argument, gratitude, and finally fear — was laid before them, and they were not moved.

## Living it

- **Ask what a thing is for.** *ʿAbath*, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's definition, is what has no value or benefit "neither in reality nor by implication." The test Hūd applies to ʿĀd's monuments is a test any of us can apply to a purchase, a project, or an afternoon: does this serve a real need, or only an image?
- **Watch for the "as if you will live forever" reflex.** On Ibn ʿAbbās's reading of ayah 129, the verse describes conduct, not creed. A person can affirm death with his tongue while every plan he makes assumes he is staying.
- **Strength is measured by what you do when you can do anything.** Ayah 130 does not condemn their power; it condemns how they used it — seizing "as tyrants," in Ibn Kathir's words, "strong, violent and tyrannical."
- **Count your blessings as evidence, not as trophies.** In ayah 132 Hūd names Allah by what He has supplied. The honest response to "with what you yourselves know" is gratitude and obedience, not the conclusion that we earned it.
- **Give sincere advice without a price on it.** Ayah 127 is the model for anyone who calls others to good: ask nothing of them, and let the reward be with the Lord of all that exists.

passages.title: ʿĀd shrug off the warning and are destroyed
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat close the story of Hud and his people, ʿĀd. Hud had warned them, encouraged them, and — as Ibn Kathir puts it — "clearly explained the truth to them." Here we hear their answer: a shrug (136), an appeal to what their ancestors always did (137), and a flat denial that any punishment is coming (138). Then, in a single short sentence, a whole civilisation is gone (139).

What holds the passage together is the speed of that fall. Their refusal takes three ayat to say; their destruction takes one clause — **فَكَذَّبُوهُ فَأَهْلَكْنَاهُمْ**, "So they denied him, and We destroyed them." Everything the passage wants you to feel lives in that gap.

## "It is all the same to us" (ayah 136)

**سَوَآءٌ عَلَيْنَآ أَوَعَظْتَ أَمْ لَمْ تَكُن مِّنَ ٱلْوَٰعِظِينَ** — "It is all the same to us whether you admonish us or are not one of those who admonish."

Ibn Kathir gives the plain sense of it: their meaning is *"we will not give up our ways."* This is not an argument. They do not answer Hud's evidence; they simply announce that no evidence will move them.

Ibn Kathir sets their words beside their answer elsewhere in the Qur'an — *"And we shall not leave our gods for your (mere) saying! And we are not believers in you"* (11:53) — and then, strikingly, beside Allah's own description of the hardened rejecter:

> **"Verily, those who disbelieve, it is the same to them whether you warn them or do not warn them, they will not believe"** (2:6)
> **"Truly, those against whom the Word of your Lord has been justified will not believe"** (10:96)

So ʿĀd's boast turns out to match Allah's verdict on such people, spoken in their own mouths. They thought they were declaring independence; they were describing their own condition. This is the sober heart of ayah 136: a person can reach a state where the reminder simply no longer lands — and be proud of it.

## "Only the way of the ancients" (ayah 137)

**إِن هَٰذَآ إِلَّا خُلُقُ ٱلْأَوَّلِينَ.** Ibn Kathir reports that this word was recited in two ways — *khuluq* and *khalq* — and that the two readings open two related meanings. Both come down from the early authorities; neither is to be dismissed.

**First reading: "nothing but the tales of the ancients."** Ibn Kathir attributes this understanding to Ibn Masʿūd, to ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās (as reported from al-ʿAwfī), and to ʿAlqamah and Mujāhid. On this reading ʿĀd are saying: *what you have brought us is nothing but the tales of the ancients.* Ibn Kathir then points out that the idolaters of Quraysh said the very same thing about what came to the Prophet ﷺ:

> *"Tales of the ancients, which he has written down, and they are dictated to him morning and afternoon"* (25:5)
> *"And when it is said to them, 'What is it that your Lord has sent down?' they say, 'Tales of the ancients!'"* (16:24)

That parallel is part of the point of telling the story at all. The line the Quraysh were using had been used before — by a people who had already been destroyed for using it.

**Second reading: "the religion of the ancients."** On this reading, says Ibn Kathir, *khuluq* means their religion: what they were following was the religion of the ancients, of their fathers and grandfathers. He paraphrases their attitude with real force: *"We are following them, we will live as they lived and die as they died, and there will be no resurrection and no judgement."*

Read together, the two meanings expose the same instinct from two sides. Truth is dismissed as old fiction; falsehood is embraced as venerable inheritance. Antiquity is treated as an argument when it suits, and as a slur when it does not. What is entirely missing is the question a serious person asks: *is it true?*

## "And we will never be punished" (ayah 138)

**وَمَا نَحْنُ بِمُعَذَّبِينَ.** Ibn Kathir joins this ayah directly to the one before it: after that paraphrase — *"we will live as they lived and die as they died, and there will be no resurrection and no judgement"* — he writes, *"Hence they said: 'And we are not going to be punished.'"* Deny the Hereafter, and the warner becomes a nuisance rather than a rescuer. They have placed themselves outside the reach of consequence. Then comes ayah 139.

## "So they denied him, and We destroyed them" (ayah 139)

Ibn Kathir explains: *"they continued to disbelieve and stubbornly oppose Allah's Prophet Hud, so Allah destroyed them."* The Qur'an does not narrate the disaster here; it states it and moves on. But Ibn Kathir gathers the details from where they are described elsewhere.

**A wind matched to their pride.** Allah sent against them a strong and furious wind — a fiercely blowing wind that was intensely cold. Ibn Kathir draws out the fittingness of it: *"the means of their destruction was suited to their nature, for they were the strongest and fiercest of people, so Allah overpowered them with something that was even stronger and fiercer than them."*

Their boast is recorded in the Qur'an: *"As for ʿĀd, they were arrogant in the land without right, and they said: 'Who is mightier than us in strength?' See they not that Allah Who created them was mightier in strength than them"* (41:15). They asked who was stronger; the answer arrived as weather.

**How long, and what it left.** Allah says *"And as for ʿĀd, they were destroyed by a furious violent wind"* — and Ibn Kathir explains **ḥusūman** in that passage (69:6-7) as meaning consecutively: seven nights and eight days. The aftermath: *"so that you could see men lying overthrown, as if they were hollow trunks of date palms"* (69:7). Ibn Kathir's comment is unsparing — they were left as headless bodies, the wind carrying a man off and dropping him on his head, then casting him aside, as if they were uprooted stems of date palms.

**Nothing they had built helped.** They used to build fortresses in the mountains and caves, and they dug ditches half as deep as a man is tall, *"but that did not help them against the command of Allah at all."* Ibn Kathir seals the point with **"Verily, the term given by Allah, when it comes, cannot be delayed"** (71:4). Ayah 138 said *we will never be punished*; ayah 139 answers in the space of a breath.

**Who ʿĀd were — and one thing they were not.** Ibn Kathir identifies these as the former ʿĀd (*"And that it is He Who destroyed the former ʿĀd"*, 53:50), descendants of Iram ibn Sām ibn Nūḥ. On **إِرَمَ ذَاتِ ٱلْعِمَادِ**, "ʿĀd of Iram, possessors of the pillars" (89:6-7), he says they used to live among pillars — and he rejects the claim that Iram was a city, noting that those who say so take the idea from Isrāʾīliyyāt narrations, that is, reports of Israelite or Jewish-Christian origin that entered the tafsir literature without sound support. Ibn Kathir traces these to the words of Kaʿb and Wahb, and says *"there is no real basis for that."* His argument rests on the wording: the next ayah says *"the like of which were not created in the land"* (89:8) — **created**, not built. Had a city been meant, Ibn Kathir notes, it would have said *"the like of which was not built in the land."* So the ayah is describing a **people** unmatched in might, power and tyranny.

That is a small lesson in method worth carrying: a great scholar checking a famous story against the wording of the Qur'an, and dropping it when the wording will not carry it.

**"Surely in this is a sign, yet most of them are not believers."** A sign was set before people — and most still did not believe. The passage quietly warns that evidence alone does not produce faith: a heart that has already said *"it is all the same to us"* can look straight at a sign and see only weather.

## "And your Lord is the Almighty, the Most Merciful" (ayah 140)

The episode closes on two of Allah's names.

**Al-ʿAzīz**, the Almighty — this is exactly the attribute the story has just demonstrated. A people who asked *"Who is mightier than us in strength?"* met the One who is mightier than them, and their fortresses and ditches counted for nothing.

**Ar-Raḥīm**, the Most Merciful — placed right beside it, on the heels of a destruction. The mercy is in the sequence Ibn Kathir described at the start: Allah sent them a messenger who *warned them, encouraged them, and clearly explained the truth to them.* Nothing fell on ʿĀd until every word had been spoken and refused. And the mercy is in the telling: this story reaches us as a warning while there is still time to act on it.

Affirm both names as they are: Allah is truly Almighty and truly Merciful, without likening His attributes to anything in creation and without emptying them of meaning. The pairing is not a contradiction to be resolved but a description of the Lord you are actually dealing with.

## Living it

**Beware the shrug.** The most dangerous thing in this passage is not the wind; it is ayah 136. "It is all the same to us" is a spiritual condition, and it creeps up on people who still attend the gathering and still hear the reminder. The test is simple: when a reminder reaches you, does anything move?

**"Everyone does it" is not evidence.** Ayah 137 is inherited habit dressed up as a reason. Custom, family practice, and what people have always done are not, by themselves, arguments — as Ibn Kathir's paraphrase makes plain: *"we will live as they lived and die as they died."*

**Nothing you build is a shelter from Allah's decree.** ʿĀd built fortresses in the mountains and caves and dug ditches, and Ibn Kathir's verdict is flat: *"that did not help them against the command of Allah at all."* Whatever we build for security — walls, savings, reputation, plans — is worth having, but it was never the thing keeping us safe. *"Verily, the term given by Allah, when it comes, cannot be delayed"* (71:4).

**And a word for whoever carries the message.** Hud warned, encouraged, and explained clearly, and was answered with a shrug. He was not a failure. The outcome was never his to secure — as ayah 139 says, *We destroyed them*, and as ayah 140 says, *your Lord is the Almighty, the Most Merciful.* Your task is to speak the truth well; what hearts do with it belongs to Allah.

passages.title: Ṣāliḥ's address to the people of Thamūd
passages.tafsir:
This passage is Ṣāliḥ's opening address to his people, Thamūd: a prophet standing among his own tribe, asking them one piercing question — do you imagine all of this is permanent? — and then telling them what to do about the answer. What holds ayat 141–152 together is a single movement: an opening claim to trust (141–145), a survey of everything they owned and enjoyed (146–149), and then a double command — obey me, do not obey them (150–152).

## Where this comes in

In Ibn Kathir's commentary, ayah 141 arrives directly after the account of Hūd and his people. Allah, he writes, "tells us how the people of Hūd responded to him after he had warned them, encouraged them, and clearly explained the truth to them" — and their answer was: *It is the same to us whether you preach or be not of those who preach.* Ibn Kathir glosses that as meaning, "we will not give up our ways." They held to the religion of their fathers and grandfathers, as if to say, in his words, "We are following them, we will live as they lived and die as they died, and there will be no resurrection and no judgement." Hence their conclusion: *And we are not going to be punished.*

They were destroyed. And then the sūrah turns, and a second prophet begins to speak to a second nation.

## Who Thamūd were, and where

Ibn Kathir tells us plainly who these people were. Allah "tells us about His servant and Messenger Ṣāliḥ, whom He sent to his people Thamūd. They were Arabs living in the city of Al-Ḥijr — which is between Wadi Al-Qura and Greater Syria. Their location is well known." They came, he adds, after ʿĀd and before Ibrāhīm, peace be upon him.

That last detail is not a footnote. Ibn Kathir also mentions that hadiths — which he had already given in his commentary on Sūrat al-Aʿrāf — describe how the Messenger of Allah ﷺ passed by the dwelling place of Thamūd when he set out toward Syria, going as far as Tabūk before returning to Madinah to prepare for the campaign. So the audience receiving this sūrah was not being told a legend about nobody in particular. This was a place on a road they knew.

## The opening (141–145)

**"Will you not have taqwā?" (142).** Ibn Kathir keeps the Arabic word *taqwā* here rather than translating it; the rendering of the ayah before us puts it as, "Will you not fear Allah?" Ṣāliḥ does not open by listing charges. He opens with a question aimed at the conscience. And Ibn Kathir summarises what he was calling them toward: their prophet "called them to Allah, to worship Him alone with no partner or associate, and to obey whatever commands were conveyed to them, but they refused, rejecting him and opposing him."

**"I am a trustworthy messenger to you" (143).** Notice what stands immediately beside this claim. Ṣāliḥ says he is trustworthy — and two ayat later he removes the one thing that would give anyone grounds to doubt it.

**"I ask you no reward" (145).** Ibn Kathir puts it directly: "He told them that he did not seek any reward from them for his call to them, but that he would seek the reward for that with Allah."

That is the whole logic of the disclaimer. A man asking for payment can be bought off, argued down, or dismissed as self-interested. Ṣāliḥ removes that escape entirely. He has no stake in their wealth, and his account is with the Lord of al-ʿĀlamīn, not with them.

## The heart of the passage: "Will you be left secure?" (146–149)

Ibn Kathir heads this section *A Reminder to Them of Their Circumstances and the Blessings They Enjoyed*, and describes what Ṣāliḥ was doing: he "preached to them, warning them that the punishment of Allah could overtake them and reminding them of the blessings that Allah had bestowed upon them, by giving them ample provision and making them safe from all kinds of dangers, giving them gardens and flowing springs, and bringing forth for them crops and fruits."

Read that list of blessings carefully — it includes *making them safe from all kinds of dangers*. So the question in ayah 146, "will you be left secure in that which you have here?", is not a denial that they had it good. Their security was real, and it was a gift. The question is about permanence: who told them the lease had no end date?

Then he itemises the estate.

**Gardens and flowing springs (147).**

**"And date palms with soft clusters" (148).** This is the phrase the early authorities lingered over. Ibn Kathir gathers the reports: al-ʿAwfī narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās that it means "ripe and rich"; ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥa narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās that it meant growing luxuriantly; and Ismāʿīl bin Abī Khālid narrated from ʿAmr bin Abī ʿAmr — who met the Companions — from Ibn ʿAbbās that it means, "When it becomes ripe and soft." Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated these, and said something similar was narrated from Abū Ṣāliḥ. The reports converge on one picture: fruit at its ripest and softest, the point a farmer waits for.

**"And you hew out in the mountains, houses with great skill" (149).** Here the commentators genuinely differ, and it is worth seeing why.

- Ibn Kathir reports that Ibn ʿAbbās and others said *fārihīn* means "with great skill," while another report from Ibn ʿAbbās gives, "They were greedy and extravagant" — which he notes was the view of Mujāhid and another group.
- Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presents the split slightly differently: it attributes to Ibn ʿAbbās the sense of *arrogant and conceited people*, while Abū Ṣāliḥ and Imām Rāghib took the word to mean *experts*.

Ibn Kathir then does something instructive — he refuses to treat the two senses as rivals: "There is no contradiction between the two views, because they built the houses which they carved in the mountains as a form of extravagant play, with no need for them as dwelling places. They were highly skilled in the arts of masonry and stone-carving, as is well known to anyone who has seen their structures."

That reconciliation is the point of the whole passage. The skill was real, and the skill was a gift. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws exactly that out: the meaning is that "Allah Taʿālā has favoured you by teaching such skills that you could make houses by cutting hills. The essence of all this is that you should remember the bounties of Allah Taʿālā and should not make mischief and trouble on earth." What was wrong was not the craftsmanship but the use it was put to — carving mountains they had no need to live in.

Note where that comment lands. *Do not make mischief and trouble on earth* is, word for word, the charge Ṣāliḥ will bring against their leaders three ayat later.

## "So fear Allah and obey me" (150)

Ayah 150 repeats ayah 144 word for word, but now it lands with the whole inventory of blessings behind it. Ibn Kathir unpacks what the command means in practice: "Pay attention to that which could benefit you in this world and the Hereafter; worshipping your Lord Who created you, who granted you provisions so that you could worship Him alone and glorify Him morning and evening."

Read that carefully. In Ibn Kathir's reading the provisions were not the goal — they were the means. The springs and the date palms were given *so that* they would be free to worship. Thamūd took the equipment and forgot the purpose.

## "And follow not the command of the extravagant" (151–152)

Ṣāliḥ finishes by naming the rival authority. Obedience is not really optional; a person will obey someone. So the two commands stand side by side: obey me (150), do not obey them (151).

Who are *al-musrifīn* — rendered here as "the extravagant," and in the translation before us as "the transgressors"? Ibn Kathir is specific: "their chiefs and leaders, who called them to Shirk, disbelief and opposition to the truth." These are not shadowy strangers. They are the men at the top of Thamūd's own society, whose approval mattered and who had every reason to keep things exactly as they were.

Ayah 152 then describes them: they "make mischief in the land, and reform not." The second half is the sharper half. It is not merely that they cause damage; setting things right never appears on their agenda at all.

## Living it

Three threads run out of this passage.

**Security is on loan.** The question of ayah 146 reaches anyone with a full fridge, a paid mortgage and a quiet street. Thamūd's safety, in Ibn Kathir's own summary, was one of Allah's blessings upon them — nothing in Ṣāliḥ's speech disparages gardens, springs or crops. What he denies is that any of it constitutes a guarantee.

**Skill is a grace, and grace can be misspent.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the ruling out of ayah 149 directly: "nice vocations are Allah's Graces, and to draw benefit from them is lawful. But if they are used for some sinful purpose or in an unlawful act, or if someone gets involved in them with unnecessary concentration, then it is not lawful to adopt them." Note that third clause — even a lawful trade becomes a problem when it swallows a person whole.

**Building beyond need.** Commenting on this same ayah, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that an example of "unnecessary construction of tall buildings and its contempt" has just been mentioned in the preceding ayat. It cites there the hadith reported by Imām Tirmidhī on the authority of Sayyidnā Anas, may Allah be pleased with him: *All spendings are in Allah's way, except construction, which has no merit* — meaning, it explains, that what is built in excess of requirement carries no benefit or virtue.

Put the threads together and Ṣāliḥ's argument is complete. Everything Thamūd had — the water, the harvest, the soft ripe dates, even the hands that could cut a house out of a cliff — came from Allah. The only question left is the one in ayah 146: did they think it came without an Owner, and without an end?

passages.title: The she-camel and the punishment of Thamūd
passages.tafsir:
This passage is the second half of the story of Ṣāliḥ (upon him be peace) and his people Thamūd: their answer to his call, the miracle they themselves specified, the rule attached to it, their breaking of that rule, and the destruction that followed. What holds ayat 153–159 together is a single word — **āyah**, "sign." In ayah 154 the people demand a sign; in ayah 155 they receive the sign they asked for; and in ayah 158, after they have destroyed it and been destroyed, Allah says that the whole affair *is* a sign. The sign they wanted was for their eyes; the sign Allah leaves behind is for the heart.

## "You are simply bewitched" (153)

Ibn Kathir opens by telling us that Allah is describing how Thamūd responded to their Prophet Ṣāliḥ, upon him be peace, when he called them to worship their Lord. Their first move is not an argument — it is a diagnosis.

**Mujahid**, one of the early authorities Ibn Kathir cites, explains the word plainly: "They meant he was one affected by witchcraft." On that reading, the charge was not that Ṣāliḥ was lying but that something had been done to him — some spell had disordered him, and that is why he was saying these strange things about one Lord and about accountability.

Notice how convenient this is. It lets them dismiss everything he says without examining a single thing he says. A man under a spell does not need to be answered — he needs to be pitied. It is a way of ending a conversation while appearing to explain it.

## "You are but a human being like us" (154)

Then comes the real objection, and it is the one that runs through the whole history of prophethood: *You are but a human being like us.*

Ibn Kathir unpacks what lies underneath the sentence. The meaning, he says, is *"how can you receive Revelation when we do not?"* It is not really a statement about Ṣāliḥ's humanity. It is a statement about their own standing. If revelation is going to land anywhere, why has it landed on him and not on us?

To show that this is a recurring reflex and not a one-off, Ibn Kathir places beside it what Thamūd are quoted as saying elsewhere in the Qur'an:

> "Is it that the Reminder is sent to him alone from among us? Nay, he is an insolent liar!" — Tomorrow they will come to know who is the liar, the insolent one! (54:25–26)

Read the two together and you can hear the pride. The objection is not "this message is false"; it is "why him?" Envy is being dressed up as reasoning. And the reply in that passage is not an argument either — it is a deadline: *tomorrow they will know*.

Having said all that, they finish with a challenge: *bring us a sign if you are of the truthful*. Ibn Kathir notes that they asked him for a sign to prove that what he had brought them from their Lord was the truth.

## The sign they designed themselves (154–155)

This is the heart of the passage, and Ibn Kathir tells the story in detail.
